newsitem.title: ITALY: Vranitzky calls for military action on Albania.
newsitem.headline: Vranitzky calls for military action on Albania.

text.p: European envoy Franz Vranitzky said on Friday he saw no alternative to Western military intervention to halt the anarchy and chaos spreading through Albania.

"I will report that there is no alternative as far as I can see," Vranitzky told reporters after separate talks with Albanian government leaders and representatives of rebel southern towns on the Italian frigate Aliseo in the Adriatic.
"The decision has to be taken very quickly," he told a news conference in the southeastern Italian port of Brindisi.

Vranitzky, the former Austrian chancellor, made clear that a request for outside military help should be made to individual governments rather than to any particular body and acknowledged that a number of states would not support such a plan.
"The idea has arisen of (creating) a coalition of the willing. That means the decision-making could be shortened with regard to the established institutions," Vranitzky said.
But in The Hague, Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok said any intervention would require United Nations approval.

"There will be no decision on an international presence without a clear mandate and the Security Council has not yet issued a mandate for international action," said Kok, whose country holds the European Union's presidency.

Vranitzky, who is acting on behalf of the 54-state Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said he had met for four hours on the Aliseo with leaders of Albania's new multi-party government of national reconciliation.

He later held 90 minutes of talks with representatives of rebel committees of several southern Albanian towns including Sarande, Gjirokaster and Vlore, hotbeds of the armed insurrection that has swept the impoverished Balkan state.

"We are now in a situation where the government, President (Sali) Berisha, political parties and rebel committees want the same goal. To restore public order, to restore democracy and to have new elections," Vranitzky said.
"In Albania there is not a civil war, there is unrest, uproar against the political solution which so many Albanians believe to be unjust," Vranitzky added.
Diplomatic sources said Vranitzky had briefed several foreign ministers on the talks by telephone, including U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini.
One source said Vranitzky told Dini the weekend should be spent finding support for sending in troops to restore order "because by themselves they (the Albanians) are not going to be able to do it".

Albania's unrest, which has spread to the north and the capital Tirana in an orgy of looting by lawless gunmen, was sparked by the collapse of shady saving schemes. Rebels in the south have turned their outrage on Berisha, insisting that he should step down.
Berisha made a major concession this week by agreeing to a new all-party government and early elections by June but has given no sign he will resign before then.
Vranitzky, who met new Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, Foreign Minister Arjan Starova and army chief of staff General Adem Copani, said the OSCE was not in a position to suggest anyone should resign.

"We have to do everything to support the government, the prime minister, the foreign minister. Because people support them, apprehensions about Berisha could become of secondary importance," Vranitzky said.
